title: Data Modelling in Microsoft Fabric: From Raw Sources to Star Schema to Semantic Model
purpose: Show how conceptual, logical, and physical data modelling decisions map onto concrete Fabric layers — medallion lakehouse staging, a dimensional (star schema) gold layer in Warehouse or Lakehouse, and a Direct Lake composite semantic model — so a designer can place data-vault-style staging, dimensional load order, and security decisions at the right layer.
accessibleSummary: An architecture diagram tracing data modelling from source systems through a medallion lakehouse into a dimensional gold layer and up into a Power BI semantic model. Source systems land in a Bronze lakehouse layer unchanged. A Silver layer cleanses and conforms that data; an inference callout notes that teams needing full historical traceability sometimes insert a data-vault-style raw staging structure (hubs, links, satellites) at this point, though Fabric has no dedicated data-vault product feature. From Silver, a fixed ETL order — stage, then dimensions, then facts, then post-processing — loads a Gold-layer dimensional model built as a star schema: dimension tables radiating around central fact tables, built either as a Warehouse or as Lakehouse materialized views. A dimension-table detail node explains surrogate keys and slowly changing dimension handling; a fact-table detail node explains grain, foreign keys to dimension surrogate keys, and the practitioner heuristic that a fact table with more than roughly 50 columns is usually hiding a dimension. The star schema feeds a Direct Lake semantic model, which can build a composite model keeping large fact tables in Direct Lake mode while smaller dimension tables use Import or DirectQuery. Two warning nodes flag real failure modes: applying row-level security at the Warehouse T-SQL layer forces Direct Lake semantic models built on that table into DirectQuery fallback, and Fabric Warehouse does not enforce foreign keys, so referential integrity between fact and dimension surrogate keys is the ETL process's responsibility, not the database's.
longDescription: This diagram grounds the conceptual/logical/physical modelling progression in the concrete Fabric implementation path Microsoft documents for dimensional modelling: source systems feed a medallion lakehouse (Bronze raw, Silver cleansed), which stages a dimensional ETL that loads dimension tables before fact tables into a Gold-layer star schema, which in turn backs a Direct Lake semantic model consumed by Power BI. It also marks where a data-vault-style raw layer is an architectural option Fabric Atlas infers from common practice (not a Microsoft Fabric product feature), and calls out two sourced failure modes: RLS-layer mismatch causing Direct Lake fallback, and Fabric Warehouse's lack of enforced foreign keys shifting referential-integrity responsibility onto the ETL layer.

nodes.label: Source systems
nodes.summary: Operational databases, SaaS APIs, files, and events that carry the raw data a dimensional model will eventually describe.
nodes.detail: Source systems are outside Fabric's modelling scope but define the conceptual model implicitly: their entities and relationships (customers, orders, products) are what the star schema will later formalize as dimensions and facts. They arrive with source-native shapes — normalized OLTP schemas, semi-structured JSON, flat files — none of which is yet a dimensional model.
nodes.whyItMatters: Getting the conceptual model right starts here: before any Fabric item exists, the business entities and events a warehouse needs to describe must be identified from these sources, or the star schema built downstream will describe the wrong things.

processing: Identify candidate business entities (conceptual model) before any physical design
Classify each source as batch, CDC, or streaming to decide ingestion pattern
Hand off to Bronze ingestion via pipelines, Spark, Dataflows Gen2, or shortcuts
outputs: Raw extracts landing in the Bronze medallion layer
drill.example: A retail chain's order-management OLTP database, a third-party pricing API, and daily point-of-sale CSV exports are the three source systems that will eventually populate a Sales star schema's Order fact and Product, Store, and Date dimensions.
controls: Ingestion cadence (batch vs. CDC vs. streaming)
Which Fabric ingestion route: pipeline copy, Spark notebook, Dataflow Gen2, or shortcut
failureModes: Skipping conceptual modelling and jumping straight to physical tables produces a schema that mirrors source system quirks instead of business meaning.

nodes.label: Bronze layer (Lakehouse)
nodes.summary: Raw data stored exactly as received, with no transformation, inside a Fabric Lakehouse.
nodes.detail: Bronze is the first medallion layer: source data lands unchanged so it can always be reprocessed if downstream logic changes. Microsoft's medallion guidance recommends linking source data into Bronze via a OneLake shortcut rather than physically copying it where possible, and treats small files here as acceptable given the raw, high-frequency nature of ingestion.
nodes.whyItMatters: Keeping Bronze byte-faithful to the source is what makes Silver and Gold reprocessable without re-extracting from the source system — a foundational reliability property for any dimensional model built on top.

evidence.note: The three medallion layers are bronze (raw, stored exactly as received with no changes), silver (enriched), and gold (curated for reporting).
For the bronze layer, source data should be linked via a OneLake shortcut rather than physically copied into the lakehouse.

processing: Land data as-is, no schema changes or cleansing
Prefer OneLake shortcuts over physical copies for external sources
Accept smaller, more frequent files given the raw ingestion pattern
outputs: Untouched raw tables/files available for Silver processing
drill.example: Daily point-of-sale CSV exports land in a Bronze lakehouse folder exactly as delivered, including any malformed rows, so Silver cleansing logic can be re-run later without re-pulling from the source.
controls: Shortcut vs. physical copy for external sources
Ingestion frequency and partitioning of raw files
failureModes: Applying transformation logic in Bronze defeats its purpose as a faithful, replayable raw copy.

nodes.label: Silver layer (cleansed)
nodes.summary: Errors fixed, formats standardized, duplicates removed — data conformed but not yet dimensionally modelled.
nodes.detail: Silver enriches Bronze data: fixing errors, standardizing formats, removing duplicates. It is the conformed, trustworthy layer that both a warehouse ETL process and ad hoc Spark analysis can build on. Microsoft's dimensional-modelling guidance explicitly treats a lakehouse's bronze, silver, or gold layer as a valid ETL source for a warehouse dimensional model, which can remove the need for a separate staging step inside the warehouse.
nodes.whyItMatters: Silver is where source-system quirks are resolved once, centrally, instead of being re-solved inside every downstream fact/dimension load — and it is the layer a data-vault-style raw staging structure would sit alongside if a team chooses that pattern.

evidence.note: Silver layer: enriched — errors fixed, formats standardized, duplicates removed.

When a Fabric lakehouse already implements a medallion architecture, its bronze, silver, or gold layer can serve directly as the ETL source for a warehouse dimensional model, making a separate staging step in the warehouse unnecessary.

processing: Fix data-quality errors and standardize formats/types
Deduplicate and conform records across sources
Optionally structure as data-vault-style hubs/links/satellites for full historical traceability
outputs: Conformed Silver tables usable as staging input for the Gold dimensional load
drill.example: Point-of-sale rows with inconsistent date formats and duplicate transaction IDs from three regional systems are standardized and deduplicated into one conformed Silver Sales table.
controls: Cleansing/deduplication rules
Whether to introduce a data-vault-style raw staging structure before conforming
failureModes: Silver output errors propagate directly into dimensional load logic downstream — the load-tables guidance depends on Silver already being trustworthy.

nodes.label: Data vault staging (optional pattern)
nodes.summary: Hub/link/satellite modelling as an architectural option for teams needing full historical auditability before dimensional modelling.
nodes.detail: Data vault is a modelling technique — hubs for business keys, links for relationships, satellites for descriptive/historical attributes — that some teams insert between Silver and Gold when regulatory or audit requirements demand every source change be traceable. Fabric has no dedicated data-vault product feature; this is Fabric Atlas's architectural interpretation of where the pattern would fit against Fabric's own medallion and dimensional-modelling guidance, not a Microsoft-documented behavior.
nodes.whyItMatters: Teams sometimes assume Fabric provides data-vault tooling out of the box; it doesn't — data vault here is table design discipline layered onto ordinary Delta tables in a Lakehouse, positioned deliberately outside the sourced medallion/dimensional path.

processing: Model business keys as hub tables
Model relationships between keys as link tables
Model descriptive/historical attributes as satellite tables with load timestamps
outputs: A fully auditable historical layer that a dimensional Gold model can be built from
drill.example: A financial-services team storing every historical version of a customer's KYC attributes uses hub/link/satellite tables in a Lakehouse before deriving the Gold-layer dimensional model, satisfying an audit requirement that plain SCD Type 2 dimensions alone would not.
controls: Whether the audit/compliance requirement justifies the added modelling and load complexity
failureModes: Adopting data vault without a genuine historical-auditability requirement adds ETL and query complexity with no offsetting benefit over a direct medallion-to-star-schema path.

nodes.label: Dimensional ETL: stage → dimensions → facts → post-process
nodes.summary: A fixed load order: staging tables, then dimension tables, then fact tables, then post-processing such as semantic-model refresh.
nodes.detail: Microsoft's load-tables guidance specifies a strict ETL order: optionally load staging tables, process dimension tables next (so surrogate keys exist), then process fact tables (which reference those surrogate keys), then run post-processing tasks like semantic-model refresh. Surrogate keys must never be regenerated via truncate-and-reload once fact tables reference them, and source deletions become soft deletes rather than physical removals.
nodes.whyItMatters: This ordering is a hard dependency, not a style preference: a fact table load requires the dimension surrogate keys it references to already exist, and getting that order wrong silently breaks foreign-key lookups.

evidence.note: A dimensional model ETL process should run in a fixed order: optionally load staging tables, then process dimension tables, then process fact tables, then run post-processing tasks like semantic model refresh.
Surrogate keys on dimension tables should never be regenerated via a full truncate-and-reload once fact tables reference them.

processing: Stage (optional): mirror source columns/types, truncate at each run
Process dimensions: apply SCD type 1/2/3 logic, assign/preserve surrogate keys
Process facts: incremental load via watermark/CDC, look up dimension surrogate keys
Post-process: refresh dependent semantic models
outputs: Loaded Gold-layer dimension and fact tables ready for the semantic model
drill.example: A nightly job truncates staging tables, applies SCD Type 2 logic to the Customer dimension so surrogate keys are stable, then incrementally loads new Order fact rows using a high-watermark on OrderModifiedDate, then triggers a semantic-model refresh.
controls: SCD type per dimension (1 overwrite, 2 versioned, 3 limited history)
Fact incremental-load mechanism: watermark, CDC, or change tracking
failureModes: Loading facts before dimensions causes dimension-key lookups to fail or resolve to stale surrogate keys.
Truncate-and-reload on a dimension table after facts already reference its surrogate keys invalidates existing fact-to-dimension relationships.

nodes.label: Gold layer: star schema (dimensions + facts)
nodes.summary: A central fact table surrounded by dimension tables, Microsoft's recommended default design for a Fabric Warehouse.
nodes.detail: The Gold layer implements the physical dimensional model: dimension tables describe business entities (products, people, places, dates), fact tables store measurable events (orders, stock balances) plus the dimension keys relating them, and a warehouse commonly contains multiple fact tables forming multiple stars. It can be built either as a Fabric Warehouse or as Lakehouse materialized views/lakehouses, per Fabric's two documented medallion deployment patterns.
nodes.whyItMatters: Star schema is called out as Microsoft's recommended default, not one option among several — it minimizes joins, benefits from indexing, and keeps future schema growth (a new attribute, fact, or dimension) structurally simple.

evidence.note: Microsoft recommends star schema (fact and dimension tables) as the design approach for building a Fabric Warehouse.

A star schema is named for its shape: one fact table sits at the center with related dimension tables radiating outward like points of a star, and a warehouse commonly contains multiple fact tables forming multiple stars.
Fabric offers two medallion deployment patterns: all three layers as separate lakehouses, or bronze/silver as lakehouses with gold implemented as a Fabric Warehouse.

inputs: Dimension and fact tables loaded by the dimensional ETL
processing: Dimension tables radiate around a central fact table (or multiple fact tables forming multiple stars)
Fact tables carry measures plus dimension surrogate keys, at one consistent grain
Built as Warehouse T-SQL tables or Lakehouse materialized lake views
outputs: A queryable dimensional model consumed by the semantic model and direct SQL clients
drill.example: A Sales star schema has one Order fact table at a line-item grain plus Customer, Product, Store, and Date dimension tables, all reachable from the fact table by a single join hop.
controls: Warehouse vs. Lakehouse materialized-view implementation of Gold
Fact table grain definition
failureModes: A fact table growing past roughly 50 columns is usually carrying dimension-like attributes that should be split out, per the practitioner heuristic.

nodes.label: Dimension table: surrogate keys + SCD
nodes.summary: Business entities with a surrogate key and slowly changing dimension (SCD) history handling.
nodes.detail: Dimension tables use a surrogate key (not the source system's natural key) as the join target for fact tables, because natural keys can change or collide across sources. Slowly changing dimension type determines how attribute changes are handled: Type 1 overwrites in place, Type 2 versions the row with new surrogate keys and validity dates, Type 3 keeps limited prior-value history alongside the current value.
nodes.whyItMatters: SCD type is a modelling decision with real consequences: Type 2 is the only one of the three that preserves point-in-time historical reporting accuracy, and it can only be built reliably in a warehouse ETL — not in Power Query alone.

evidence.note: Slowly changing dimension handling differs by type: SCD type 1 updates existing attribute values in place, SCD type 2 expires the current row version and inserts a new versioned row, and SCD type 3 updates attributes in place but preserves limited prior-value history.
Power Query alone cannot implement a Type 2 slowly changing dimension; that change-detection logic must run upstream, typically in a data warehouse ETL/load process.

inputs: Conformed Silver attribute data for one business entity
processing: Assign or reuse a stable surrogate key independent of source natural keys
Detect attribute changes against the current dimension row
Apply SCD Type 1 (overwrite), Type 2 (new versioned row), or Type 3 (limited history) logic per attribute
outputs: A dimension table joinable to fact tables via surrogate key
drill.example: A Customer dimension tracks region changes with SCD Type 2: when a customer moves region, the old row is expired and a new row with a new surrogate key and updated region is inserted, preserving historical sales-by-region accuracy.
controls: SCD type chosen per attribute or per dimension
Late-arriving/inferred-member handling
failureModes: Regenerating surrogate keys via truncate-and-reload after facts reference them breaks existing fact-to-dimension relationships and can make SCD Type 2 history unrecoverable.

nodes.label: Fact table: grain + foreign keys
nodes.summary: Measurable events at one consistent grain, referencing dimension surrogate keys — with no enforced foreign keys in Fabric Warehouse.
nodes.detail: Fact tables store measures (order amounts, quantities) at one fixed grain plus the dimension surrogate keys needed to relate them. Fabric Warehouse does not enforce foreign key constraints, so referential integrity between fact rows and dimension surrogate keys is the ETL process's responsibility, not the database engine's. A practitioner heuristic holds that a fact table with more than roughly 50 columns is usually carrying attributes that belong in a dimension instead.
nodes.whyItMatters: Because the warehouse itself won't catch a broken fact-to-dimension reference, ETL-level integrity checks (or an explicit 'Unknown member' fallback row) are the only real safety net against silently orphaned fact rows.

evidence.note: Because Fabric Warehouse does not enforce foreign keys, the ETL process itself is responsible for referential integrity checks when loading fact rows against dimension surrogate keys.
When a fact row's dimension key lookup fails, the row should still be inserted using a special 'Unknown' dimension member rather than being dropped.
A well-structured Power BI model should not mix dimension and fact roles in a single table, and fact tables should always load data at a consistent grain.

inputs: Dimension tables with resolved surrogate keys
processing: Define and hold to one fixed grain (e.g. one row per order line)
Look up dimension surrogate keys for each fact row
Insert an 'Unknown member' row rather than dropping rows on a failed key lookup
Load incrementally via watermark, CDC, or change tracking rather than full reload
outputs: A fact table joinable to every related dimension via surrogate keys
drill.example: An Order fact table loads at order-line grain; a line item whose Product surrogate-key lookup fails is still inserted, pointed at an 'Unknown Product' dimension row, so the sale isn't silently dropped from revenue totals.
controls: Fact grain definition
Unknown-member fallback behavior on failed key lookups
failureModes: A fact table exceeding roughly 50 columns is a practitioner signal that dimension-like attributes should be split out.
Because Fabric Warehouse enforces no foreign keys, a missing ETL integrity check lets orphaned fact rows accumulate silently.

nodes.label: Semantic model (Direct Lake composite)
nodes.summary: A Power BI semantic model reading the star schema directly from OneLake via Direct Lake, with large fact tables in Direct Lake and small dimensions optionally in Import mode.
nodes.detail: A dimensional model built in a Fabric Warehouse or Lakehouse Gold layer is the recommended prerequisite for an enterprise-grade Power BI semantic model. Direct Lake on OneLake supports composite models: very large fact tables stay in Direct Lake mode to avoid refresh cost, while smaller dimension tables can use Import or DirectQuery in the same model, and table type (fact vs. dimension) in the model is determined by relationship cardinality, not any explicit property.
nodes.whyItMatters: Composite modelling lets the physical star schema map cleanly onto the semantic layer without forcing every table into the same storage mode — the large fact table gets Direct Lake's no-import freshness while small, frequently-joined dimensions can still use Import for maximum interactivity.

evidence.note: A dimensional model built in a Fabric Warehouse is the recommended prerequisite for an enterprise-grade Power BI semantic model.
Direct Lake on OneLake supports composite models, so very large fact tables can stay in Direct Lake mode (avoiding refresh cost) while dimension tables use Import or DirectQuery in the same model.
In a Power BI semantic model, whether a table behaves as a dimension or a fact table is determined entirely by relationship cardinality, not by any explicit table property.

inputs: Gold-layer star schema (Delta tables in OneLake)
processing: Load large fact tables in Direct Lake mode, reading Delta columns from OneLake on demand
Optionally load small dimension tables in Import mode for maximum interactivity
Resolve one active relationship per table pair; role-playing dimensions get their own table
outputs: A composite semantic model consumed by Power BI reports and DAX queries
drill.example: A 500-million-row Order fact table stays in Direct Lake mode while the 200-row Store dimension is switched to Import, giving instant slicer interactions on Store without losing Direct Lake freshness on the fact table.
controls: Per-table storage mode in a composite model
Which relationship is active per table pair (USERELATIONSHIP for alternates)
failureModes: Applying row-level security at the Warehouse T-SQL layer on a table this model reads forces the model into DirectQuery fallback instead of Direct Lake.

nodes.label: Warning: RLS at the wrong layer breaks Direct Lake
nodes.summary: T-SQL row-level security on a Warehouse table forces dependent Direct Lake semantic models into DirectQuery fallback.
nodes.detail: Row-level security is recommended at the semantic-model layer for Power BI consumption; T-SQL-layer row-level security in the Warehouse is reserved for direct Warehouse access by non-Power-BI clients, because applying RLS at the T-SQL layer on a table causes Power BI Direct Lake semantic models built on that table to fall back to DirectQuery mode.
nodes.whyItMatters: Choosing the wrong security layer silently degrades every Direct Lake model built on that table to DirectQuery performance — a real, sourced trap for teams that reflexively apply RLS at the database layer out of habit.

evidence.note: Row-level security is recommended at the semantic-model layer for Power BI consumption, while T-SQL-layer row-level security in the Warehouse is reserved for direct Warehouse access by non-Power-BI clients.

Applying row-level security at the T-SQL layer on a Fabric Warehouse table causes Power BI Direct Lake semantic models built on that table to fall back to DirectQuery mode; the recommended fix is to implement RLS at the semantic-model layer instead.

inputs: A Gold-layer Warehouse table backing a Direct Lake semantic model
processing: T-SQL RLS predicate applied at the Warehouse table
Direct Lake semantic model detects the incompatible security layer at query time
Model falls back silently to DirectQuery against the SQL analytics endpoint
outputs: A working but permanently slower DirectQuery model instead of Direct Lake
drill.example: A team adds T-SQL RLS to a Sales fact table so non-Power-BI SQL clients see only their region's rows; every Power BI report built on that table's Direct Lake model silently drops into DirectQuery performance.
controls: Choose semantic-model RLS for Power BI consumers; reserve T-SQL RLS for direct non-Power-BI SQL access
failureModes: The fallback is silent — nothing errors, reports just get slower — so teams often don't notice until performance complaints surface.

nodes.label: Warning: no enforced foreign keys in Warehouse
nodes.summary: Fabric Warehouse does not enforce foreign key constraints, so fact-to-dimension referential integrity is the ETL's job.
nodes.detail: Because Fabric Warehouse does not enforce foreign keys, the ETL process itself is responsible for referential integrity checks when loading fact rows against dimension surrogate keys. Unlike a traditional RDBMS where a bad foreign key insert simply fails, an unmatched fact-to-dimension key silently produces an orphaned or dropped row unless the ETL explicitly checks for it.
nodes.whyItMatters: Teams migrating from a database that enforces foreign keys can assume Warehouse gives the same safety net; it doesn't, so integrity checking has to be built into the dimensional ETL rather than assumed as a platform guarantee.

evidence.note: Because Fabric Warehouse does not enforce foreign keys, the ETL process itself is responsible for referential integrity checks when loading fact rows against dimension surrogate keys.

inputs: Fact rows with dimension surrogate-key references
processing: ETL performs its own key-existence check against dimension tables
No database-level constraint rejects an unmatched key
Failed lookups routed to an 'Unknown member' row rather than silently dropped
outputs: Fact rows guaranteed to reference a valid (possibly 'Unknown') dimension row
drill.example: A late-arriving Order row references a ProductId not yet present in the Product dimension; without an explicit ETL check, that row could silently vanish from revenue reports instead of being flagged or mapped to 'Unknown Product'.
controls: Explicit referential-integrity check step in the dimensional ETL
Unknown-member fallback design
failureModes: Assuming Warehouse enforces foreign keys the way a traditional RDBMS does leads to silently missing fact rows with no error raised.

walkthrough.title: 1. Source systems define the conceptual model
walkthrough.explanation: Before any Fabric item exists, the business entities and events worth modelling are identified from source systems — this is the conceptual model, done in your head or on a whiteboard, not in a Fabric item.

walkthrough.title: 2. Bronze: land raw data unchanged
walkthrough.explanation: Source data lands in a Lakehouse Bronze layer exactly as received, ideally via a OneLake shortcut, so it stays replayable if downstream logic changes.

walkthrough.title: 3. Silver: cleanse and conform
walkthrough.explanation: Errors are fixed, formats standardized, duplicates removed — Silver becomes the trustworthy staging source for the dimensional ETL, and Microsoft explicitly allows Silver to serve as that staging layer directly.

walkthrough.title: 3b. Optional: data-vault staging for full auditability
walkthrough.explanation: Teams with strict historical-auditability requirements sometimes insert hub/link/satellite modelling here — an architectural option Fabric Atlas infers from common practice, not a Microsoft Fabric feature.

walkthrough.title: 4. Load in a fixed order: stage, dimensions, facts, post-process
walkthrough.explanation: Microsoft's documented load order matters because fact rows need dimension surrogate keys to already exist — get this order wrong and key lookups fail.

walkthrough.title: 5. Gold: the physical star schema
walkthrough.explanation: The Gold layer is the physical model: dimension tables radiating around central fact tables, Microsoft's recommended default design for a Fabric Warehouse.

walkthrough.title: 5a. Dimension tables: surrogate keys + SCD
walkthrough.explanation: Dimension tables use surrogate keys and slowly changing dimension logic to track historical attribute changes accurately.

walkthrough.title: 5b. Fact tables: grain + unenforced foreign keys
walkthrough.explanation: Fact tables hold measures at one grain plus dimension surrogate keys — but Fabric Warehouse enforces none of those foreign keys, so integrity checking is the ETL's job.

walkthrough.title: Warning: no database-level referential integrity
walkthrough.explanation: A missing ETL integrity check on fact loads lets orphaned fact rows accumulate silently, since the Warehouse itself won't reject them.

walkthrough.title: 6. Semantic model: composite Direct Lake
walkthrough.explanation: The star schema backs a Power BI semantic model; large fact tables can stay in Direct Lake mode while small dimensions optionally use Import, in one composite model.

walkthrough.title: Warning: security at the wrong layer breaks Direct Lake
walkthrough.explanation: T-SQL row-level security on the underlying Warehouse table silently forces the Direct Lake model into DirectQuery fallback — row-level security belongs at the semantic-model layer instead.
